unit_label: Foundations of Learning, Creativity and Design Thinking

questions.q: How many modes does the Stanford d.school design thinking model have?
options: Three
Four
Five
Six
questions.explain: The d.school model has exactly five modes: Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype and Test. Each one has its own job, from understanding users to checking a prototype with them. Three-phase models come from IDEO's human-centred design toolkits, not from the d.school.
why_wrong: Three is the number of phases in IDEO's human-centred design models (for example Hear, Create, Deliver), not the number of d.school modes.
Four leaves out one of the modes. The d.school keeps Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype and Test as five separate modes.
Six adds an extra mode such as Implement or Assess, and the d.school model has no such mode.

questions.q: In the d.school model, which mode comes immediately after Ideate?
options: Define
Prototype
Test
Empathize
questions.explain: The order is Empathize → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test. Once the team has generated many ideas in Ideate, it turns the chosen ones into quick, rough prototypes. Those prototypes then go to users in Test.
why_wrong: Define comes before Ideate. It produces the problem statement that ideation then works on.
Test comes after Prototype, because users need something to try before anything can be tested.
Empathize is the first mode. A team may loop back to it, but it is not the next mode in the sequence.

questions.q: What is the main output of the Define mode?
options: A long list of possible solution ideas for the team to choose from
A rough paper or cardboard model of the solution
Notes on how users reacted when they tried a prototype
A point-of-view (POV) problem statement naming the user, their need and the insight behind it
questions.explain: Define turns the raw material gathered in Empathize into one focused, actionable problem statement. It is often written as a point of view: user + need + insight. This gives ideation a clear target. Idea lists, prototypes and user feedback all come from later modes.
why_wrong: A list of solution ideas is the output of Ideate, which comes after Define.
A rough physical model is the output of Prototype.
User reactions to a prototype are gathered in Test, the last mode.

questions.q: What is the main aim of the Ideate mode?
options: To interview users about their experiences
To choose and build the one final product
To generate a wide range of possible solutions
To observe how users react to a prototype
questions.explain: Ideate is about going wide: the team generates many possible solutions to the defined problem before narrowing down. Quantity comes first because more ideas give more chances of finding a good one. Interviewing users belongs to Empathize, and watching users react belongs to Test.
why_wrong: Interviewing users is an Empathize activity.
Ideate goes wide instead of committing to one final product. Design thinking then builds rough prototypes and tests them rather than building the final product straight away.
Observing how users react to a prototype happens in Test.

questions.q: In the d.school model, what does a team typically make in the Prototype mode?
options: A fully working version of the final product, ready to launch
Quick, cheap, rough versions of its ideas, such as paper sketches or cardboard mock-ups, for users to try
A written report describing the users' needs
A detailed engineering drawing ready for manufacture
questions.explain: In the Prototype mode the team turns the ideas chosen in Ideate into quick, cheap, rough versions, such as paper screens, a cardboard model or a storyboard, that users can try in Test. These versions exist to learn from, not to launch, so the team does not mind changing them or throwing them away. If testing shows a problem, the team loops back and builds again.
why_wrong: A finished, working product is not what the Prototype mode makes. Prototypes are rough versions built to learn from before anything is settled.
A report on users' needs comes from Empathize and Define, before there is any idea to prototype.
A drawing ready for manufacture treats the design as settled. The Prototype mode makes rough versions for users to try, so the design can still change.

questions.q: What does VARK stand for?
options: Visual, Analytical, Reflective, Knowledge
Verbal, Aural, Rational, Kinesthetic
Visual, Active, Read/write, Knowledge
Visual, Aural, Read/write, Kinesthetic
questions.explain: VARK names four preferred ways of taking in information: Visual (diagrams, charts, graphs), Aural (listening and discussion), Read/write (written text) and Kinesthetic (hands-on practice and real examples). A learner can have more than one of these preferences.
why_wrong: In VARK, A is Aural (not Analytical), R is Read/write (not Reflective) and K is Kinesthetic (not Knowledge).
V is Visual, not Verbal, and R is Read/write, not Rational.
A is Aural, not Active, and K is Kinesthetic, not Knowledge.

questions.q: Which mode of thinking is relaxed and broad, letting the brain make new connections in the background?
options: Focused mode
Diffuse mode
Convergent thinking
Rote learning
questions.explain: Diffuse mode is the relaxed, wide-ranging state (on a walk, in the shower, just before sleep) in which the brain links ideas that seem unrelated. Focused mode is the opposite: deliberate concentration on a known approach. Good problem solving switches between the two.
why_wrong: Focused mode is deliberate, narrow concentration on a known approach, the reverse of this description.
Convergent thinking narrows many options down to one best answer. It is not relaxed background association.
Rote learning means memorising by repetition. It is not a relaxed mode that forms new connections.

questions.q: What is innovation?
options: Any new idea that someone has just thought of
Creating a device that has never existed before, whether or not anyone uses it
Putting a new idea into practice so that it creates value
Filing a patent for a new product
questions.explain: Innovation is implementation that produces value: a new idea actually put into use by real people, with a real benefit. It does not need new technology. A new payment or delivery model built on existing products can be an innovation. A new idea on its own is creativity, and a new device on its own is an invention.
why_wrong: A new idea that has only been thought of is creativity. It becomes an innovation only once it is implemented and produces value.
Creating something new that nobody uses is an invention, not an innovation.
A patent protects an invention. Filing one does not put the idea into use or create value.

questions.q: What is functional fixedness?
options: A mental block in which a person sees an object only in its usual use
The fear of sharing ideas in case they are criticised
The habit of noticing only evidence that supports what you already believe
Working on a problem for hours without taking any breaks
questions.explain: Functional fixedness is a cognitive block that ties an object to its familiar function, so other uses go unseen. An example is never thinking of a coin as a screwdriver. It limits creativity because useful resources get overlooked. Asking 'what else could this be used for?' helps break it.
why_wrong: Fear of criticism is an emotional block (fear of failure), not functional fixedness.
Noticing only the evidence that supports your view is confirmation bias.
Working without breaks describes staying stuck in focused mode. It is not a block about how objects can be used.

questions.q: Which of these best defines creativity?
options: The ability to memorise large amounts of information
Copying a successful product exactly
Following a fixed procedure step by step without change
The ability to produce ideas that are both new and useful
questions.explain: Creativity is generating ideas that are novel and also useful or appropriate to the problem. Novelty alone is not enough: a random idea that solves nothing is not creative in this sense. Creativity supplies the ideas that invention and innovation later build on.
why_wrong: Memorising information is recall. It does not produce new ideas.
An exact copy produces nothing new, so it lacks the novelty that creativity requires.
Following a fixed procedure without change is routine work and generates no new ideas.

questions.q: The idea of 'wicked problems' in design is most closely associated with:
options: Herbert Simon
IDEO
Horst Rittel
The Stanford d.school
questions.explain: Horst Rittel introduced the term 'wicked problems' for planning and design problems that are ill-defined, have no single right answer and have no clear point at which they are finished. Design thinking is often presented as an approach suited to such problems.
why_wrong: Herbert Simon is known for describing design as changing existing situations into preferred ones, not for naming wicked problems.
IDEO is a design firm known for popularising human-centred design, not for coining the term 'wicked problems'.
The Stanford d.school is known for the five-mode design thinking model, not for the term 'wicked problems'.

questions.q: What does it mean to say that design thinking is human-centred?
options: It starts from whatever technology the organisation already has
It starts from understanding the needs of the people who will use the solution
It can be carried out only by trained designers
It is used only to improve the look of a product
questions.explain: Human-centred means the process begins with, and keeps coming back to, the people who will use the solution: their needs, behaviour and feelings. That is why Empathize is the first mode. Technology and appearance still matter, but they serve those needs rather than driving the process.
why_wrong: Starting from the technology you already have is technology-driven, the opposite of human-centred.
Non-designers use design thinking too. 'Human-centred' is about whose needs sit at the centre, not about who does the work.
Design thinking solves problems for people. It is not limited to styling how a product looks.

questions.q: Which word best describes how the design thinking process moves through its stages?
options: Linear and one-pass
Random, with no order to the stages
Top-down, decided by management alone
Iterative
questions.explain: Design thinking is iterative: teams loop back to earlier modes whenever testing or new insights show that something needs rethinking. A prototype that fails a test can send the team back to Ideate, Define or even Empathize. Each loop improves both the understanding of the problem and the solution.
why_wrong: Linear and one-pass describes a pipeline completed once in strict sequence. Design thinking loops back.
The modes have a clear logical order and purpose. Going back to an earlier mode is deliberate, not random.
Design thinking is driven by users' needs and testing with users, not by decisions made from the top alone.

questions.q: How did Herbert Simon describe design?
options: Devising courses of action aimed at changing existing situations into preferred ones
Making products look attractive
Producing detailed technical drawings
The last stage of manufacturing a product
questions.explain: Herbert Simon described design very broadly: anyone who devises a course of action to change an existing situation into a preferred one is designing. On this view design covers services, policies and processes as well as objects. This broad view is why design thinking can be applied to many kinds of problem.
why_wrong: Appearance is only a small part of design. Simon's definition is about changing situations, not styling.
Technical drawings are one output of engineering work, not Simon's definition of design.
Simon treated design as purposefully planning a change, not as a final manufacturing step.

questions.q: Which sequence gives the d.school modes in the correct order?
options: Empathize → Ideate → Define → Prototype → Test
Define → Empathize → Ideate → Prototype → Test
Empathize → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test
Empathize → Define → Prototype → Ideate → Test
questions.explain: First you understand users (Empathize). Then you turn that understanding into one focused problem statement (Define), generate ideas for it (Ideate), build rough versions (Prototype) and try them with users (Test). Each mode feeds the next: ideas need a defined problem, and testing needs a prototype.
why_wrong: This puts Ideate before Define, so ideas would be generated for a problem the team has not yet agreed on.
This puts Define before Empathize, so the problem would be defined before the team understands its users.
This puts Prototype before Ideate, but you cannot build a prototype before generating the ideas it represents.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five d.school design thinking modes?
options: Ideate
Implement
Define
Test
questions.explain: The five modes are Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype and Test. Implementation does appear as a phase in one version of IDEO's three-phase model, but Implement is not a d.school mode. Adding a sixth mode to the d.school list is a common mistake.
why_wrong: Ideate is the third d.school mode, where the team generates many ideas.
Define is the second d.school mode. It produces the point-of-view problem statement.
Test is the fifth d.school mode, where users try the prototypes.

questions.q: Which pairing of activity and d.school mode is correct?
options: Interviewing users about their daily routine — Ideate
Brainstorming dozens of possible solutions — Define
Writing a point-of-view statement — Test
Building a paper mock-up of an app screen — Prototype
questions.explain: A paper mock-up is a rough, cheap model built to learn from, which is exactly what the Prototype mode is for. Interviewing users belongs to Empathize, brainstorming to Ideate, and writing a POV statement to Define.
why_wrong: Interviewing users builds understanding of them, which is Empathize, not Ideate.
Brainstorming solutions is Ideate. Define narrows findings into a problem statement, not a list of solutions.
A POV statement is the output of Define. Test is where users try a prototype.

questions.q: Which statement about the VARK model is accurate?
options: VARK is a reason to present material in varied forms, but matching teaching to one preference has not been shown to improve achievement
Matching teaching to each student's VARK preference has been shown to reliably raise their marks and exam scores
Each learner can take in information only through their single preferred VARK mode, so other forms are wasted on them
A higher score on one VARK letter shows that a learner is more intelligent than someone with a lower score
questions.explain: VARK describes preferences for how people like to receive information. Research has not shown that matching teaching to a student's preferred style improves achievement, so the safe use of VARK is to present ideas in several forms. A preference does not limit how someone can learn, and it does not measure ability.
why_wrong: The evidence does not support the claim that matching teaching to a VARK preference raises achievement.
Preferences are not limits. People learn through all four modes, and many have more than one preference.
VARK describes how a person prefers to receive information, not how intelligent they are.

questions.q: Which task is best suited to focused mode rather than diffuse mode?
options: Taking a walk so an unexpected link between two ideas can surface
Letting the mind drift to make loose, broad associations
Checking a circuit design line by line against its specification
Stepping away from a hard problem and returning later with a fresh angle
questions.explain: Focused mode is deliberate concentration on a known approach, which is what precise checking and verification need. The other three options are diffuse-mode activities. They are relaxed, broad and happen in the background, which helps form new connections but is poor for exact checking.
why_wrong: A relaxed walk that lets new links surface is diffuse mode.
Loose, broad association is the defining feature of diffuse mode.
Stepping away lets diffuse mode work in the background. The fresh angle comes from diffuse thinking, not focused thinking.

questions.q: Which pairing of a VARK preference and a study activity is correct?
options: Aural — discussing a topic aloud or listening to a recorded lecture
Visual — reading long paragraphs of text
Read/write — building a working physical model
Kinesthetic — studying a flowchart
questions.explain: Aural learners prefer information that is heard or spoken, so discussion and recorded lectures suit them. Diagrams and flowcharts suit Visual learners, written text suits Read/write learners, and hands-on practice with real examples suits Kinesthetic learners.
why_wrong: Reading paragraphs of text is Read/write. Visual refers to diagrams, charts and graphs.
Building a physical model is hands-on, which makes it Kinesthetic.
A flowchart is a diagram, which fits Visual, not Kinesthetic.

questions.q: Which option correctly matches creativity, invention and innovation?
options: Creativity: putting ideas into practice for value · Invention: producing new ideas · Innovation: creating a new device
Creativity: producing new, useful ideas · Invention: creating something new · Innovation: putting a new idea into practice so it creates value
Creativity: creating a new device · Invention: putting it into practice for value · Innovation: producing new ideas
All three mean the same thing: having a new idea
questions.explain: Creativity generates new and useful ideas. Invention creates something new. Innovation puts a new idea into practice so that it produces value for people. Innovation does not need an invention: a new payment model built on existing technology can be an innovation, while a patented device nobody uses is only an invention.
why_wrong: This swaps the terms. Putting ideas into practice for value is innovation, and creating a new device is invention.
This swaps the terms. Creating a new device is invention, and producing new ideas is creativity.
The terms are distinct. An idea that is never built or used is neither an invention nor an innovation.

questions.q: A new engine design is patented but never manufactured or used by anyone. How is it best classed?
options: An innovation, because it is new technology
Both an invention and an innovation
An invention, but not an innovation
Neither, because a patented design is still only an idea
questions.explain: Something new has been created, so it is an invention. Innovation requires implementation that produces value, meaning real use by real people, and this design has never been put into practice. Novelty or new technology alone does not make something an innovation.
why_wrong: New technology is not enough. An innovation needs the idea to be put into use so that it creates value.
It cannot count as an innovation until it is implemented and produces value, and that has not happened.
A patented design is a new thing that has been created, which makes it an invention, not merely an idea in someone's head.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of functional fixedness?
options: Keeping quiet in a meeting for fear an idea will be laughed at
Paying attention only to feedback that agrees with your own view
Rejecting an idea because 'that is not how things are done here'
Not thinking of using a coin as a screwdriver because a coin is 'for paying'
questions.explain: Functional fixedness ties an object to its usual function, so other possible uses go unseen: the coin stays 'money' and is never seen as a tool. The other options are different blocks. Fear of ridicule is an emotional block, favouring agreeable feedback is confirmation bias, and 'not how things are done here' is a cultural block.
why_wrong: Fear of being laughed at is an emotional block (fear of failure), not a block about how an object can be used.
Paying attention only to agreeable feedback is confirmation bias.
Rejecting an idea because of custom or tradition is a cultural block.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts design thinking with a linear engineering pipeline?
options: Design thinking loops back to earlier modes when testing reveals something new; a linear pipeline moves through its stages once, in sequence
Design thinking goes through each mode exactly once; a linear pipeline repeatedly loops back to earlier stages
Both are one-pass processes and differ only in the number of stages they contain
Design thinking leaves out testing, while a linear pipeline always ends with it
questions.explain: Design thinking is iterative: a failed test can send the team back to Ideate, Define or Empathize, and these loops are expected. A linear pipeline is planned as a single forward pass, with each stage finished before the next begins. What separates them is the loop, not the number of stages.
why_wrong: This reverses the two. Design thinking is the one that loops back, while a linear pipeline is a single forward pass.
Design thinking is not one-pass. Its modes are repeated whenever testing reveals something new.
Test is one of the five design thinking modes, so design thinking does not leave testing out.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a feature of a wicked problem?
options: It has no single, definitive formulation
It has one correct answer that can be checked and confirmed
It has no clear point at which it is finished
Its solutions are better or worse rather than simply right or wrong
questions.explain: Horst Rittel described wicked problems as ill-defined: they have no definitive formulation, no clear stopping point, and solutions that can only be judged better or worse. A problem with one checkable right answer is a well-defined ('tame') problem, the opposite of a wicked one.
why_wrong: Having no definitive formulation is a defining feature of a wicked problem.
Having no clear stopping point is a defining feature, because there is always room to do better.
Solutions being judged better or worse, not true or false, is a defining feature of a wicked problem.

questions.q: A team builds a canteen pre-order app based only on what the developers think students want. No student is interviewed or observed. After launch, students ignore pre-ordering because they decide what to eat only after seeing the food at the counter. Which d.school mode did the team skip that would have shown them this before a single idea was generated?
options: Define
Test
Empathize
Prototype
questions.explain: In Empathize the team observes and interviews real users to learn how they actually behave. Watching students at the counter would have shown that they choose food by sight, and that kills the pre-order idea before anything is built. Designing from the builders' own assumptions is exactly the mistake that the human-centred Empathize mode prevents.
why_wrong: Define turns what was learnt in Empathize into a problem statement. With no user research there was nothing to turn into one, so the missing input comes from Empathize.
Testing would catch it, but only after an idea had been chosen and built. The question asks which mode shows it before any idea exists.
A prototype is built after ideation, so it cannot show how users behave before any idea exists.

questions.q: In Test, students use a prototype app for booking library seats without any difficulty. But several of them explain that they avoid the library for a different reason: it closes at 8 pm, before they have finished evening classes and dinner. What is the best next step in the d.school model?
options: Keep polishing the booking app in Prototype, since it tested well
Treat the project as finished, because Test is the final mode
Run a new Ideate session for more booking-app features on the same problem statement
Go back to Define and reframe the problem statement around the new insight about opening hours
questions.explain: Design thinking is iterative. Test does more than check a solution: it can show that the problem itself was framed wrongly. Here the prototype works, but the real barrier is the opening hours, so the POV written in Define no longer matches the users. The team loops back to Define to restate the need with this insight, then ideates again from there.
why_wrong: The app works, but it solves the wrong problem. Refining it further does nothing about why students stay away.
Test is the last mode in the list, not the end of the process, and its findings often send teams back to earlier modes.
New features on the same POV keep solving the old problem, when the insight shows that the POV itself is wrong.

questions.q: A student spends two hours staring at a circuit problem and gets nowhere. She gives up and goes for a walk, and on the way back a new approach suddenly occurs to her. Which explanation fits best?
options: Focused mode kept running at full strength during the walk and finally found the answer
Diffuse mode kept working on the problem in the background and made a connection that concentration had blocked
She overcame functional fixedness by learning a new fact during the walk
Her kinesthetic VARK preference meant that the walk taught her the answer
questions.explain: Focused mode concentrates on one known path. When that path is wrong, more effort just repeats the same dead end. Stepping away lets diffuse mode, which is relaxed, broad background thinking, link the problem to more distant ideas. The sudden idea on the walk is that background connection coming to the surface.
why_wrong: Focused mode is deliberate concentration, and relaxing on a walk is the opposite, so this swaps the two modes.
She learnt nothing new on the walk and did not reimagine any object's use. Functional fixedness is about seeing an object only in its usual role.
Kinesthetic means learning through hands-on work with the material. A walk that involves no circuit teaches nothing about the circuit.

questions.q: A student reasons: 'New insights come from diffuse mode, so I'll skip studying the chapter and just relax until the answers come to me.' Why will this plan fail?
options: Diffuse mode works on material that focused study has already loaded, so with no groundwork it has nothing to connect
Diffuse mode works only for Visual learners in the VARK model
Relaxing switches the brain into focused mode, which blocks creative insight
Diffuse mode is only for checking and verifying work, not for producing new ideas
questions.explain: The two modes work as a pair. Focused study loads the concepts and the problem, and then diffuse mode links them in new ways during rest. Skip the focused part and the background processing has no raw material, so no insight arrives.
why_wrong: VARK preferences are about how a person likes information to be presented. They have nothing to do with which thinking mode is available.
This swaps the modes: relaxing is what brings in diffuse mode, not focused mode.
This is backwards. Checking and precise work are focused-mode tasks, and diffuse mode is where new connections form.

questions.q: After a relaxed evening walk, an idea for fixing a bug in her project suddenly comes to a student. The project is due for grading tomorrow. What should she do next, and in which mode?
options: Stay in diffuse mode and submit at once, because ideas from diffuse mode are already verified
Stay in diffuse mode and keep relaxing, because checking details is a diffuse-mode task
Switch to focused mode and drop the idea, because only focused mode produces reliable ideas
Switch to focused mode and carefully test and check the fix before submitting
questions.explain: Diffuse mode is good at producing new connections, but it gives no guarantee that they are correct. Focused mode, which is deliberate step-by-step concentration, is the right tool for checking and precise work. The productive pattern is to let diffuse mode find the idea and then switch to focused mode to test it.
why_wrong: Diffuse mode produces connections but does not check them. An insight can feel right and still be wrong.
This swaps the modes: careful checking of details is focused-mode work.
Focused mode is for checking the idea, not throwing it away. The diffuse insight is valuable and just needs testing.

questions.q: A student calls herself a 'visual learner' because she learns best by reading the bullet-point text on lecture slides and rewriting it as lists in her notebook. In VARK terms, which preference does this behaviour actually show?
options: Visual
Aural
Read/write
Kinesthetic
questions.explain: VARK classifies how information is presented, not which sense organ takes it in. Printed words (lists, notes, text on slides) belong to Read/write, even when they are read off a screen. Visual in VARK means graphical forms such as diagrams, charts and flowcharts, so reading and rewriting bullet points is a Read/write preference.
why_wrong: In VARK, Visual means diagrams, charts, maps and graphs, where information is shown as shapes and layouts. Printed words do not count as Visual just because they are seen.
Aural is learning by listening and discussing. She is reading and writing, not listening.
Kinesthetic is learning through hands-on practice and real examples. Rewriting notes is text-based, not hands-on.

questions.q: A student sketches an idea for a folding study desk (stage 1). She then builds a working model and patents it (stage 2). Two years later a furniture company licenses the design, and hostels start buying and using the desk (stage 3). At which point does it first count as an innovation?
options: Stage 1, when the original idea was conceived
Stage 2, when a working model exists and the patent is granted
Stage 3, when it is put into use and produces value for buyers and users
Never, because a folding desk uses no new technology
questions.explain: The three ideas follow in sequence here: creativity is the idea, invention is the new thing actually made, and innovation is that thing put into practice so that it produces value. A patent proves the design is new, not that anyone uses it. Implementation plus value happens only when hostels buy and use the desk, so stage 3 is where it becomes an innovation.
why_wrong: An idea is creativity. At this point nothing has been made or used.
A working, patented model is an invention: new and actually created. But nobody has adopted it yet, so it has produced no value in use.
Innovation does not need new technology. It needs implementation that creates value, and that happens in stage 3.

questions.q: Which of these problems is best described as a wicked problem?
options: Timetabling end-term exams for thousands of students so that no student has two papers at the same time
Reducing stress among students across a large university
Calculating the maximum load a steel beam of known size can carry
Finding the shortest route between two hostels on a campus map
questions.explain: Rittel's wicked problems have no agreed definition and many stakeholders who disagree. They also have no clear stopping point, and their solutions are only better or worse, never right or wrong. Student stress fits: its causes are tangled, every intervention shifts the problem, and no test can say it is solved. The other tasks may be difficult, but each has a clear goal and an answer that can be checked, so they are tame.
why_wrong: It is large and hard, but tame: the goal is clear, and any timetable can be checked for clashes and found right or wrong.
This is a textbook calculation with a clear method and one correct answer. Nothing about it is poorly defined.
This is well defined, with a single best answer that can be checked. Size or difficulty alone does not make a problem wicked.

questions.q: Two teams are designing a better water-bottle holder for hostel bunk beds. Team X spends three weeks on a detailed CAD model before showing it to anyone. Team Y makes a cardboard-and-tape version in an hour, watches students use it that evening, and changes it the next day. Which design thinking principle is Team Y following?
options: Prototype early and cheaply, so you learn from users quickly and can afford to fail
Perfect the design before users see it, so their first impression is good
Complete each mode once in strict order, never repeating any
Rely on the designers' own expertise rather than on users' reactions
questions.explain: Design thinking favours rough, fast prototypes because their job is to help the team learn, not to impress anyone. A one-hour cardboard version can be tested the same day and thrown away without regret, so mistakes show up while they are cheap to fix. Team X will find the same flaws only after three weeks of work, when changing course costs far more.
why_wrong: This is Team X's approach. It delays learning and makes every flaw expensive to fix after three weeks of work.
Team Y is going round prototype, test and change again and again. That is iteration, not a single strict pass.
Team Y does the opposite: it changes the design based on watching real students use the holder.

questions.q: Why is an iterative design thinking approach better suited to a wicked problem than a linear, one-pass engineering pipeline?
options: Because iteration guarantees that the single correct solution will eventually be found
Because wicked problems are simply larger, and iteration lets a team split them into small tame parts that are each solved once
Because trying solutions changes the team's understanding of the problem itself, so the problem has to be reframed as the work goes on
Because a linear pipeline cannot use prototypes at all
questions.explain: A wicked problem cannot be fully defined before solving starts, because each attempted solution reveals more about what the problem really is. A linear pipeline fixes the problem statement at the start and runs forward, so it has no way to absorb that learning. Design thinking's loops, in which testing sends the team back to Define or Empathize, are built for exactly this moving target.
why_wrong: Wicked problems have no single correct solution, only better or worse ones, so no method can guarantee one.
Size is not what makes a problem wicked. Its definition keeps shifting, so it cannot be cleanly split into fixed parts that are each solved once.
Linear pipelines can build prototypes too. The real difference is whether what the team learns can send it back to redefine the problem.

questions.q: By Herbert Simon's view of design, which of these people is designing?
options: A civil engineer calculating the current stress in an existing bridge to report on its condition
A physicist measuring the speed of sound in air
A surveyor counting how many students live in each hostel block
A hostel warden reorganising the mess queue so that students wait less at lunchtime
questions.explain: Simon described design as devising courses of action aimed at changing existing situations into preferred ones. The warden sees the current state (long waits), pictures a preferred one (shorter waits) and devises a change to get there. That is design, even though no product or drawing is involved. The engineer, the physicist and the surveyor are all describing things as they are now.
why_wrong: Despite the engineering job, this is analysis: it describes how the bridge is now and devises no change toward a better state.
Science describes how the world is, and measuring a quantity changes no situation.
Counting records the existing situation, and no course of action toward a better one is devised.

questions.q: Which description fits focused mode?
options: Relaxed thinking that makes broad, loose connections between ideas
Concentrated attention on one specific task, using established neural pathways
Daydreaming with no task in mind at all
Generating as many unusual ideas as possible without judging them
questions.explain: Focused mode is concentrated, logical and sequential thinking on a specific task, such as solving equations, writing code or following a procedure. The relaxed, associative kind of thinking is diffuse mode.
why_wrong: That describes diffuse mode, the opposite of focused mode.
Focused mode is the opposite of an unfocused drift; it is directed at a task.
Producing many unjudged ideas is divergent brainstorming, not a thinking mode in this unit's sense.

questions.q: According to the unit, what should you do when you are stuck on a problem you have already worked hard on?
options: Keep pushing in focused mode until it gives way
Switch to a different VARK learning style
Take a break so that diffuse processing can work on it
Ask the group to vote on an answer
questions.explain: The practical rule is to alternate focused and diffuse modes. When stuck, step away so the diffuse mode can make broader connections among material you have already struggled with.
why_wrong: The unit's rule is to alternate modes, not to grind in one of them.
Changing learning style is not the unit's advice for being stuck, and VARK has weak evidence behind it.
A vote does not solve a problem the team has not understood yet.

questions.q: Which activity is the best example of diffuse-mode thinking?
options: Solving equations step by step
Analysing a data set by following a set procedure
Writing code to a fixed specification
Brainstorming and making unexpected connections between ideas
questions.explain: Diffuse mode is creative, exploratory and associative, and the unit lists brainstorming, unexpected connections, creative writing and innovative design. Equations, data analysis and coding are focused-mode tasks.
why_wrong: Step-by-step equations are the unit's example of focused mode.
Following procedures to analyse data is listed under focused mode.
Writing code is another of the unit's focused-mode examples.

questions.q: Which statement about the diffuse mode is correct, according to the unit?
options: It reorganises material you have already struggled with, so it needs earlier focused work
It works best on an empty mind, so you should relax before ever studying
It replaces focused mode once you become an experienced designer
It can solve a problem you have never looked at, if you only relax enough
questions.explain: The unit says the diffuse mode does not work on an empty mind. It reorganises material you have already struggled with, so the order is struggle first, then step away.
why_wrong: This is the opposite of the unit's rule that diffuse mode needs prior struggle.
Neither mode replaces the other; effective problem-solving alternates between them.
A problem you have never worked on gives the diffuse mode nothing to reorganise.

questions.q: A student reads a hard problem once, makes no attempt at it, and goes for a long walk expecting the answer to arrive. Which part of the unit's rule did she skip?
options: Walking with a group, since diffuse thinking needs company
Struggling with the problem in focused mode first, since diffuse mode only reorganises material you have already worked on
Choosing a walk that matches her VARK style
Staying in focused mode for the whole session without breaks
questions.explain: The diffuse mode needs raw material. Because she never struggled with the problem, there is nothing for the break to reorganise. The rule is to struggle first, then step away.
why_wrong: The unit says nothing about needing company for diffuse thinking.
VARK is not part of the focused and diffuse rule.
The rule actually asks for breaks; refusing them is the opposite mistake.

questions.q: The unit says Mendeleev is said to have arranged the periodic table after dreaming about it. Why does the story fit the unit's rule about diffuse mode?
options: He solved it purely by dreaming, with no earlier work, which shows diffuse mode alone is enough
He used a visual learning style to see the table
He had spent days working on the problem in focused mode before the idea came
He brainstormed the arrangement with a group
questions.explain: The story is not an example of effortless inspiration. The unit stresses that he first spent days on the problem in focused mode, and the diffuse processing worked on that material.
why_wrong: The point of the story is the opposite; the days of focused work came first.
VARK is not mentioned in the Mendeleev example.
The unit presents it as individual focused work followed by a dream, not group brainstorming.

questions.q: What does Activity 1.1 ask you to do?
options: Score eight statements from 1 to 5 to find your VARK letters
List the uses of a plastic bucket by property
Walk one route across campus and find three well-designed and three badly designed things
Track for one week where and when your best ideas actually arrive, with your activity, time and mental state
questions.explain: Activity 1.1 is the idea-tracking activity. The VARK scoring is Activity 1.2, and the campus walk is Activity 1.6. The bucket technique appears as a worked example, not as Activity 1.1.
why_wrong: That is Activity 1.2, the VARK self-assessment.
The bucket property technique is a worked example about functional fixedness.
That is Activity 1.6, Design Detective.

questions.q: In the VARK model, what does the letter R stand for?
options: Reading/Writing
Reflective
Recall
Remembering
questions.explain: VARK stands for Visual, Auditory, Reading/Writing and Kinesthetic. R is the style that prefers books, notes and written material.
why_wrong: Reflective is not one of the four VARK styles.
Recall is not a VARK style, though retrieval practice is a study strategy.
Remembering is not a VARK style.

questions.q: Which VARK style prefers diagrams, charts, videos and images?
options: Auditory
Visual
Reading/Writing
Kinesthetic
questions.explain: The Visual style learns through diagrams, charts, videos and images. Auditory prefers listening and discussion, Reading/Writing prefers books and notes, and Kinesthetic prefers practical, hands-on experience.
why_wrong: Auditory learners prefer listening and discussion.
Reading/Writing prefers books, notes and written material.
Kinesthetic learners prefer practical, hands-on experience.

questions.q: In the VARK self-assessment of Activity 1.2, which two statements are added together to score K (Kinesthetic)?
options: Statements 1 and 5
Statements 2 and 6
Statements 4 and 8
Statements 3 and 7
questions.explain: The pairing is V = 1 + 5, A = 2 + 6, R = 3 + 7 and K = 4 + 8.
why_wrong: 1 + 5 scores V, the Visual style.
2 + 6 scores A, the Auditory style.
3 + 7 scores R, the Reading/Writing style.

questions.q: What does the unit say about the claim that being taught in your preferred VARK style improves your results?
options: It has been confirmed by every controlled study
It holds for kinesthetic learners but not for the other three styles
The unit does not discuss the evidence for it
The stronger claim has repeatedly failed to hold up in controlled studies
questions.explain: The unit calls VARK a useful prompt for reflecting on how you study, but says the claim that teaching in your preferred style improves results has repeatedly failed to hold up in controlled studies.
why_wrong: The unit says the opposite about controlled studies.
The unit does not single out any style as an exception.
There is a specific note headed 'A Note on Evidence' on exactly this point.

questions.q: Which three study strategies does the unit say do replicate in research?
options: Retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving
Highlighting, re-reading and summarising
Matching study to a visual, auditory or kinesthetic style
Focused mode, diffuse mode and brainstorming
questions.explain: The unit names retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving as the three study strategies that do replicate, in contrast with matching teaching to a learning style.
why_wrong: These are not the three strategies the unit names.
Style matching is exactly the claim that failed to replicate.
These are thinking modes and an idea technique, not study strategies in the unit's list.

questions.q: Why does a note on VARK evidence belong in a Design Thinking course, according to the unit?
options: VARK is the model designers use to classify users in the Empathize stage
An idea that is not research-backed can still become very popular, and what people say they want is not always what works
Designers must teach their users in each user's preferred style
VARK is proven to improve learning and so supports the design process
questions.explain: The unit treats the VARK result as a nudge toward self-awareness, not a rule. The deeper lesson is the gap between what people believe or say and what actually works, a theme that returns in Unit 2.
why_wrong: VARK is not an Empathize-stage tool in this course.
The unit makes no such claim about teaching users.
The unit says the evidence for this claim has repeatedly failed.

questions.q: Karan scores highest on K, so he decides to study only by building things and to skip notes and self-testing. Which advice fits the unit best?
options: Keep to kinesthetic study only, since matching your style improves results
Ignore the result completely, because VARK has no value at all
Treat the result as a prompt for self-awareness, but also use retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving
Retake the questionnaire until the four scores are equal
questions.explain: The unit calls VARK a useful prompt but not a rule, and points to three strategies that do replicate. So he can use the result for self-awareness while adding retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving.
why_wrong: The claim that style matching improves results has not held up.
The unit does say VARK is a useful prompt for reflection, so it is not worthless.
Equal scores are not a goal; the questionnaire is just a self-awareness prompt.

questions.q: In the candle problem described in the unit, how can the matchbox be used?
options: As a mirror that reflects light onto the wall
As a wick for the candle
It cannot be reused, so the candle has to be held by hand
As a candle holder tacked to the wall
questions.explain: Most people treat the matchbox only as storage for matches, which is functional fixedness. Seeing it as a holder tacked to the wall breaks that fixedness.
why_wrong: The unit does not describe it as a mirror.
A matchbox cannot serve as a wick.
The point is exactly that the matchbox can be reused for a new purpose.

questions.q: Which of these is a non-obvious use of a paper clip given in the unit?
options: SIM card ejector
Pen refill
Bookbinding thread
Hair dryer nozzle
questions.explain: The unit lists a cable organiser, zipper pull, SIM card ejector, reset tool, bookmark and keychain holder as everyday alternative uses of a paper clip.
why_wrong: A pen refill is not one of the unit's examples.
Bookbinding thread is not one of the unit's examples.
A hair dryer nozzle is not one of the unit's examples.

questions.q: What technique does the unit recommend for beating functional fixedness on an object such as a plastic bucket?
options: List as many uses as you can until you run out
Stop thinking about the object and list its properties, then find a use for each property
Ask users what they want the bucket to do
Combine the bucket with a second everyday object
questions.explain: Students usually list six or seven uses and stall. Listing properties such as hollow, watertight, rigid, stackable and handled, then finding a use for each, produced many more uses.
why_wrong: This is the approach that makes people stall after six or seven uses.
Asking users is research, not the property technique.
Combining objects is not the technique the worked example uses.

questions.q: In the plastic bucket worked example, how many uses did six properties produce?
options: Six
Twenty
Twenty-eight
Forty-two
questions.explain: The unit states that six properties produced twenty-eight uses, compared with the six or seven uses most students list before stalling.
why_wrong: Six is the number of properties, not the number of uses.
Twenty is not the figure the unit gives.
Forty-two is not the figure the unit gives.

questions.q: In the bucket worked example, which property led to the idea of a megaphone?
options: It is hollow
It is watertight
It has a handle
It amplifies sound
questions.explain: The unit points out that 'megaphone' only appeared once an acoustic property was named, something nobody thinks of when they picture a bucket. That is what breaking fixedness feels like.
why_wrong: Hollow led to uses such as storage, a drum or a plant pot.
Watertight led to a fish tank, ice bucket or emergency water store.
A handle led to a carrying frame, hanging planter or tool caddy.

questions.q: A team needs a way to reach a high shelf and has only a plastic bucket. Which property from the unit's worked example points to a stool or a step?
options: It is rigid and strong
It is hollow
It is watertight
It has a handle
questions.explain: The rigid and strong property gave the uses stool, step to reach a shelf, wheel chock and table base. Hollow gave storage uses, watertight gave water-holding uses and the handle gave carrying uses.
why_wrong: Hollow leads to storage, drum or plant pot, not a step.
Watertight leads to fish tank, ice bucket or water store.
A handle leads to carrying frame, hanging planter or tool caddy.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the four common cognitive blocks named in the unit?
options: Information overload
The expertise trap
Learning-style mismatch
Brain dominance
questions.explain: The four blocks are fear of failure, conformity, premature judgment and the expertise trap.
why_wrong: Information overload is not one of the unit's four blocks.
A learning-style mismatch is not one of the unit's four blocks.
Brain dominance is not one of the unit's four blocks.

questions.q: A team member says nothing about her idea because she is sure others will laugh at it. Which cognitive block is this?
options: Conformity
Premature judgment
Fear of failure
The expertise trap
questions.explain: Fear of failure is hesitation to propose ideas because of fear of criticism.
why_wrong: Conformity is following conventional thinking in order to fit in.
Premature judgment is rejecting ideas before exploring them fully.
The expertise trap is over-reliance on past solutions.

questions.q: Which block is described as over-reliance on past solutions, so that the more you know the more you reach for what worked before?
options: Fear of failure
Conformity
Premature judgment
The expertise trap
questions.explain: The expertise trap is the unit's name for leaning on past solutions, and the irony is that knowing more makes it stronger.
why_wrong: Fear of failure is about criticism.
Conformity is about fitting in.
Premature judgment is about rejecting ideas too early.

questions.q: In a meeting, several people privately think of different ideas but all agree with the first suggestion, because they want to fit in. Which block is at work?
options: Conformity
Premature judgment
Fear of failure
The expertise trap
questions.explain: Conformity is following conventional thinking in order to fit in, which is exactly what agreeing with the first suggestion to avoid standing out amounts to.
why_wrong: Nobody is rejecting an idea early; they are agreeing to fit in.
Fear of failure is about fear of criticism when proposing, not agreeing to fit in.
The expertise trap is about reaching for earlier solutions, not about group fit.

questions.q: A student crosses out her own idea the moment it occurs to her, before writing it down or exploring it. Which block is this?
options: Conformity
Premature judgment
Fear of failure
The expertise trap
questions.explain: Premature judgment is rejecting ideas before exploring them fully, and here she does it to her own idea.
why_wrong: There is no group she is trying to fit in with.
She is not worrying about others' criticism; she judges the idea herself.
She is not relying on a past solution.

questions.q: According to the unit, how does Design Thinking break these cognitive blocks?
options: By matching each person's work to their VARK learning style
By keeping experts out of the team
Through empathy, experimentation, collaboration and structured creative problem-solving
By staying in focused mode for the whole project
questions.explain: The unit's Design Thinking link says empathy, experimentation, collaboration and structured creative problem-solving break the blocks.
why_wrong: VARK matching is not the unit's remedy.
The unit does not recommend excluding experts.
Focused mode alone would not remove fear of failure or conformity.

questions.q: Which of these is the unit's example of an innovation?
options: Imagining a drone delivery system
The first telephone, by A. G. Bell
A sketch of a flying car that is never built
The iPhone reshaping the smartphone market
questions.explain: Innovation is successfully implementing creative ideas to create value, and the iPhone reshaping the smartphone market is the unit's example. Imagining a drone delivery system is creativity, and Bell's telephone is invention.
why_wrong: Imagining a drone delivery system is the unit's example of creativity.
The first telephone is the unit's example of invention.
An unbuilt sketch has not been implemented or delivered value, so it is not innovation.

questions.q: Which sentence matches the unit's claim about creativity and innovation?
options: Creativity becomes innovation only when it delivers value
Creativity and innovation mean the same thing
Innovation is creativity that has been patented
Innovation requires something entirely new that did not exist before
questions.explain: The unit's line is that creativity becomes innovation only when it delivers value. Something entirely new is the definition of invention, not innovation.
why_wrong: The unit separates the three concepts carefully.
A patent is not the test; delivering value is.
That is the definition of invention.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of incremental invention in the unit?
options: Netflix replacing DVD rental stores
USB to USB Type-C
Uber replacing traditional taxi services
Airbnb challenging the hotel industry
questions.explain: Incremental invention is a small but meaningful improvement to an existing product, such as USB to Type-C, mobile phones to smartphones or petrol cars to hybrids. The other three are disruptors.
why_wrong: Netflix is the unit's disruptor of DVD rental stores.
Uber is the unit's disruptor of traditional taxis.
Airbnb is the unit's disruptor of the hotel industry.

questions.q: Which statement about disruptive innovation is correct?
options: It makes small improvements to an existing product or process
It protects incumbent firms by supporting their current customers
It transforms markets with simpler, cheaper or more accessible solutions and focuses on unmet customer needs
It always starts by inventing something entirely new
questions.explain: Disruptive innovation is a new product, service or business model that transforms markets with simpler, cheaper or more accessible solutions. It creates new markets and challenges incumbents.
why_wrong: Small improvements describe incremental invention.
Disruptive innovation challenges incumbents rather than protecting them.
It does not need to be a brand-new invention; it can be a new business model.

questions.q: Which disruptor-and-replaced pairing matches the unit?
options: Netflix replaced traditional taxi services
Airbnb replaced DVD rental stores
Uber replaced the hotel industry
Uber replaced traditional taxi services
questions.explain: The unit pairs Netflix with DVD rental stores, Uber with traditional taxi services and Airbnb with the hotel industry.
why_wrong: Netflix replaced DVD rental stores, not taxis.
Airbnb replaced the hotel industry, not DVD rentals.
Uber replaced taxis, not hotels.

questions.q: Which option correctly labels (1) Bell's first telephone, (2) imagining a drone delivery system and (3) the iPhone reshaping the smartphone market?
options: Invention, creativity, innovation
Innovation, invention, creativity
Creativity, innovation, invention
Invention, innovation, creativity
questions.explain: The first telephone is invention because it was entirely new. Imagining drone delivery is creativity, the ability to generate original and useful ideas. The iPhone reshaping the market is innovation because the idea was implemented to create value.
why_wrong: This swaps all three labels.
This labels the telephone as creativity, but it was a new thing that did not exist before.
This labels the drone idea as innovation, but it was only imagined and not implemented.

questions.q: A company launches a cheaper, simpler product that customers who were once ignored can finally afford, and it slowly begins to challenge the market leaders. What is this?
options: Incremental invention
Disruptive innovation
Functional fixedness
Creativity without innovation
questions.explain: A simpler, cheaper, more accessible solution that creates a new market and challenges incumbents is the unit's definition of disruptive innovation.
why_wrong: Incremental invention is a small improvement to an existing product, not a market-changing model.
Functional fixedness is a cognitive block, not a type of innovation.
The product is already launched and delivering value, so it has moved beyond creativity alone.

questions.q: Which kind of problem has clear goals, constraints and one correct answer?
options: An ill-defined problem
A wicked problem
A well-defined problem
A divergent problem
questions.explain: Well-defined problems, such as equations, puzzles and technical fixes, have clear goals and constraints and a single correct answer.
why_wrong: Ill-defined problems have unclear goals or paths and many possible solutions.
Wicked problems are complex and interconnected, judged better or worse, not right or wrong.
'Divergent problem' is not one of the unit's three kinds of problem.

questions.q: Which of these is the unit's example of an ill-defined problem?
options: Solving a set of equations
Reducing climate change
Completing a logic puzzle
Designing an app or a marketing strategy
questions.explain: Ill-defined problems have unclear goals or paths and many possible solutions, and the unit gives app design and marketing strategy as examples. Equations and puzzles are well-defined, and climate is wicked.
why_wrong: Equations are the unit's well-defined example.
Climate is the unit's wicked example.
Puzzles are well-defined, with one correct answer.

questions.q: How are solutions to wicked problems judged, according to the unit?
options: As better or worse, not right or wrong
As correct or incorrect against a single answer key
By whether they meet every constraint exactly
They cannot be judged at all
questions.explain: Wicked problems are complex and interconnected, and their solutions are better or worse rather than right or wrong. Climate, poverty and healthcare are the unit's examples.
why_wrong: A single answer key belongs to well-defined problems.
Exact constraints are a feature of well-defined problems.
They can be judged; the scale is just better or worse.

questions.q: Classify these three: (a) a marketing strategy for a new café, (b) reducing climate change, (c) solving 2x + 5 = 11.
options: (a) wicked, (b) ill-defined, (c) well-defined
(a) ill-defined, (b) wicked, (c) well-defined
(a) well-defined, (b) wicked, (c) ill-defined
(a) ill-defined, (b) well-defined, (c) wicked
questions.explain: A marketing strategy has many possible solutions, so it is ill-defined. Climate change is complex and interconnected, so it is wicked. The equation has one correct answer, so it is well-defined.
why_wrong: This swaps the first two kinds.
A marketing strategy has no single correct answer, and an equation is not ill-defined.
Climate change is not well-defined, and an equation is not wicked.

questions.q: Why does the unit say Design Thinking exists?
options: Well-defined problems no longer exist in industry
Engineers lack the technical skills to solve problems
Engineering training suits well-defined problems, but ill-defined and wicked problems do not yield to the same methods
Linear methods are slower than iterative ones for every kind of problem
questions.explain: The unit says traditional engineering education trains you superbly on well-defined problems, and Design Thinking exists because the other two kinds do not yield to the same methods.
why_wrong: The unit does not say well-defined problems have disappeared.
The unit praises engineering training for well-defined problems.
The unit makes no such sweeping claim about speed.

questions.topic: History and Definition of Design Thinking
questions.q: How does the unit define Design Thinking?
options: A linear engineering pipeline in which each phase is finished before the next
A technique for generating as many ideas as possible without judging them
A method for measuring how many users do something
A human-centred approach to innovation and problem-solving that emphasises understanding users' needs and experiences
questions.explain: Design Thinking is a human-centred approach built on iterative processes and creative methods, putting the user at the centre of every decision.
why_wrong: That describes the waterfall approach it is contrasted with.
That describes brainstorming, which is one technique within it.
That describes quantitative research.

questions.topic: History and Definition of Design Thinking
questions.q: Which of these is one of the three beliefs of Design Thinking in the unit?
options: Failure early is cheaper than failure late
Ideas improve by being argued, not tested
Problems are best understood by experts, not users
Failure should be avoided at all costs
questions.explain: The three beliefs are that problems are best understood from the user's side, that ideas improve by being tested and not argued, and that failure early is cheaper than failure late.
why_wrong: The unit says ideas improve by being tested, not argued.
The unit says problems are best understood from the user's side.
The unit values early, cheap failure.

questions.topic: History and Definition of Design Thinking
questions.q: In the unit's timeline, who coins the term 'wicked problems' in the mid-1960s?
options: Herbert Simon
Rittel
Nigel Cross
Rowe
questions.explain: The timeline places the design methods movement in the mid-1960s, with Rittel coining 'wicked problems'. Herbert Simon follows in the late 1960s and 1970s with design as a way of thinking.
why_wrong: Herbert Simon is placed later, with design as a way of thinking.
Nigel Cross is placed in 1982 to 87 with Designerly Ways of Knowing.
Rowe is placed with publishing Design Thinking, not with wicked problems.

questions.topic: History and Definition of Design Thinking
questions.q: Which statement agrees with the unit's timeline?
options: The d.school was established in 1991, before IDEO was founded in 2005
Rittel coined 'wicked problems' after the d.school was established
IDEO was founded in 1991, and the Stanford d.school was established in 2005
Nigel Cross published Designerly Ways of Knowing in the mid-1960s
questions.explain: On the timeline, Rittel and the design methods movement come in the mid-1960s, Simon in 1969 to the 1970s, Cross and Rowe in 1982 to 87, IDEO in 1991 and the d.school in 2005.
why_wrong: This reverses the two dates.
'Wicked problems' were coined in the mid-1960s, long before 2005.
Cross's book is placed in 1982 to 87, not the mid-1960s.

questions.topic: History and Definition of Design Thinking
questions.q: In Lawson's experiment as the unit describes it, how did designers differ from scientists?
options: Designers analysed the problem thoroughly before proposing any solution, while scientists tested many solutions rapidly
Designers worked alone and scientists worked in teams
Designers copied existing solutions and scientists invented new ones
Designers were solution-focused, creating and testing many solutions rapidly, while scientists analysed the problem thoroughly before proposing solutions
questions.explain: Scientists were problem-focused, and designers were solution-focused and learned through iteration.
why_wrong: This reverses the two groups.
The unit says nothing about solo versus team work.
The unit says nothing about copying versus inventing.

questions.topic: History and Definition of Design Thinking
questions.q: Two teams get the same vague brief. Team A spends two weeks analysing the problem before sketching anything. Team B sketches several rough solutions on day one and tests them with users. Which team works in the mode Lawson's experiment found in designers?
options: Team B, because designers are solution-focused and learn through iteration
Team A, because designers analyse thoroughly before proposing solutions
Neither, because designers copy existing solutions
Both, because the mode depends only on the brief
questions.explain: Lawson found that designers create and test many solutions rapidly, learning as they iterate. Team A is behaving like the problem-focused scientists.
why_wrong: Thorough analysis first is the scientists' pattern.
The unit does not describe designers as copying solutions.
The experiment contrasts two ways of working, not a single brief-dependent way.

questions.q: What does the dashed arrow in the d.school diagram show?
options: A shortcut that skips the Define stage
Testing feeds back into earlier stages such as empathy, so the process is iterative and not linear
The order is fixed and the team may never return to an earlier stage
The end of the project once testing is finished
questions.explain: The unit says the dashed arrow is the whole point: testing feeds back into empathy, so the d.school process is iterative and not linear.
why_wrong: The arrow does not skip any stage.
The arrow shows the opposite of a fixed one-way order.
The arrow shows looping back, not stopping.

questions.q: Which three lenses make up the IDEO human-centred design framework?
options: Empathy, ideation and prototyping
Usability, novelty and price
Desirability, feasibility and viability
Desirability, profitability and sustainability
questions.explain: IDEO's three overlapping lenses ask whether people want it (desirability), whether it can be built (feasibility) and whether it is economically sustainable (viability).
why_wrong: Those are stages of the d.school process, not IDEO's lenses.
Those are not the unit's three lenses.
Only desirability is shared; the other two lenses are feasibility and viability.

questions.q: In the IDEO framework, which question does viability ask?
options: Do people want this?
Can we build this?
Is it new to the market?
Is it economically sustainable?
questions.explain: Viability asks whether the idea is economically sustainable. Desirability asks if people want it, and feasibility asks if it can be built.
why_wrong: That is the desirability question.
That is the feasibility question.
Novelty is not one of the three lenses.

questions.q: Where does the unit place genuine innovation in the IDEO diagram?
options: Where desirability, feasibility and viability all overlap
Where any single lens is strongest
Where desirability and feasibility overlap, even without viability
Outside the circles, in new territory
questions.explain: The unit says meeting only one or two conditions produces a concept that fails in practice, and genuine innovation lies where all three overlap.
why_wrong: One strong lens is not enough.
Without viability the idea fails in practice.
Innovation sits at the centre where the circles overlap.

questions.q: A team builds a technically brilliant, affordable product that is easy to manufacture, but customers do not want it. Which IDEO lens did the team fail?
options: Feasibility
Desirability
Viability
Iteration
questions.explain: Customers not wanting it is a desirability failure. The product is buildable (feasible) and affordable (viable), so those lenses are met.
why_wrong: It is easy to manufacture, so feasibility is met.
It is affordable, so viability is not the issue described.
Iteration is not one of the three IDEO lenses.

questions.q: How does the unit describe the relationship between the Stanford d.school and IDEO frameworks?
options: They are rivals, and the d.school model replaced IDEO's
They are identical models with different names
They are complementary lenses, not rivals
d.school is for products, and IDEO is only for services
questions.explain: The unit's conclusion says the two are complementary lenses. The d.school describes a five-stage iterative process, and IDEO describes three conditions an innovation must meet.
why_wrong: The unit does not present them as rivals.
They are different models: one describes a process and the other three conditions.
The unit makes no such split between products and services.

questions.q: In a traditional waterfall process, when does user feedback arrive?
options: Only at the very start
Continuously after every phase
Never, as users are not involved
At the end, so changes are costly
questions.explain: In waterfall each phase is finished before the next, so user feedback comes at the end, when changes are costly. Human-centred design brings in feedback continuously.
why_wrong: The unit says feedback comes at the end, not the start.
Continuous feedback is the human-centred design approach.
Users do give feedback in waterfall, just late.

questions.q: Which pair correctly contrasts waterfall with human-centred design?
options: Waterfall is linear, with Plan, Build, Test and Ship in order, while human-centred design is iterative, with empathy, prototyping and testing in a loop
Waterfall is iterative and user-focused, while human-centred design is linear
Both are linear, but human-centred design has more phases
Waterfall relies on continuous user feedback, while human-centred design collects it at launch
questions.explain: Waterfall is linear and step-by-step, with feedback late. Human-centred design is iterative and user-focused, with empathy, continuous feedback, prototyping and refinement throughout.
why_wrong: This reverses the two approaches.
Human-centred design is not linear.
This swaps when each approach gathers feedback.

questions.q: A team plans a hostel complaint app. They spend three months writing specifications, six months building it, and ask students for feedback only at launch. Which approach is this, and what is the main risk?
options: Human-centred design; too much feedback slows delivery
Waterfall; feedback comes at the end, so changes are costly
Waterfall; it skips the build phase
Human-centred design; it ignores implicit needs
questions.explain: Finishing each phase before the next and asking users only at launch is waterfall. The risk is that late feedback makes changes expensive.
why_wrong: Human-centred design asks for feedback throughout, not only at launch.
The team does build; the issue is when feedback arrives.
This is not human-centred design, since users come in only at the end.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: In 2009, Airbnb's bookings were low and revenue was flat. What did the founders do?
options: Cut the price of every listing
Hired a data team to model booking patterns
Flew to New York, visited hosts and photographed the listings themselves
Ran a large advertising campaign
questions.explain: The data showed what was happening but not why. The founders visited hosts, found amateur photographs were discouraging bookings, rented a camera and took professional photos.
why_wrong: Pricing is not part of the case.
The case is about direct observation, not more data modelling.
Advertising is not part of the case.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: What did Airbnb's founders discover when they visited hosts in New York?
options: Prices in New York were too high
Hosts were not replying to messages
The website was too slow to load
Listings had poor-quality, amateur photographs that discouraged bookings
questions.explain: Direct observation revealed the poor listing photographs, which the data alone had not explained.
why_wrong: Prices are not the finding of the case.
Unanswered messages are not part of the case.
Website speed is not part of the case.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: The unit says the photography fix 'does not scale', which is exactly why nobody had tried it. What is the lesson?
options: A hands-on, empathy-driven intervention can reveal what data cannot, even when it will not scale
Interventions that do not scale should be avoided
Data analysis alone is always enough to find the cause
Professional photographs raise bookings in every market
questions.explain: The case shows direct observation uncovering a cause the data could not, and the unit points out the fix is simple but does not scale.
why_wrong: The case argues the opposite.
The data said what was happening but not why.
The unit does not generalise to every market.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the reasons the unit gives for the failure of Google Glass?
options: Social concerns about being recorded
A very short battery life
No clear use case
A price of $1,500
questions.explain: The unit lists social concerns, awkward design, no clear use case and the $1,500 price. Battery life is not mentioned.
why_wrong: Social concerns about recording are listed.
No clear use case is listed.
The $1,500 price is listed.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: Why does the unit mention Glass Enterprise Edition?
options: It shows technical innovation alone guarantees success
It shows consumers eventually accepted Glass
The same technology worked for a different user, so a product is good or bad for someone
It shows Google lowered the price to $1,500
questions.explain: Google relaunched Glass for warehouse and factory technicians who need both hands free and do not mind how it looks. Same technology, different user, different verdict.
why_wrong: The case shows the opposite, that technology without desirability fails.
The relaunch was for workers, not the consumer market.
$1,500 was the original price that contributed to the failure.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: What was the real problem that Aravind Eye Care set out to solve about cataract surgery?
options: A new surgical technique had to be invented
Patients refused to have the surgery
Artificial lenses did not exist anywhere
Access: cost, distance and a shortage of surgeons, not the medicine
questions.explain: Cataract surgery already existed and worked. The unit says the problem was not medical but access, since the surgery cost more than most rural patients earned in months, hospitals were far away and surgeons were scarce.
why_wrong: The surgery already existed and worked.
The unit does not say patients refused it.
Lenses were not the issue; Aravind manufactured them locally to cut cost.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: Which industry did Dr. V study as a design reference for Aravind?
options: Fast food, as in McDonald's serving millions of people the same product consistently and cheaply
Airlines
Hotels
Retail banking
questions.explain: Dr. V asked how McDonald's serves millions the same product consistently, cheaply and anywhere, and studied the assembly line. The unit calls this analogous inspiration.
why_wrong: Airlines are not part of the case.
Hotels are not part of the case.
Banking is not part of the case.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: In Aravind's model, what is cross-subsidy pricing?
options: Free patients are treated by different surgeons from paying patients
Paying patients choose a tier of comfort, not of surgical quality, and this helps fund free care
Surgeons are paid by the number of operations they perform
Donors decide which patients are treated
questions.explain: Paying patients choose a comfort tier, while the surgery and the surgeons are the same for everyone. The hospital is self-sustaining without donations.
why_wrong: The unit says free patients receive the same surgery and surgeons.
Payment per operation is not described.
The hospital is financially self-sustaining without donations.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: In Aravind's approach, what is task-shifting?
options: Moving surgeons between hospitals every week
Sending patients to cheaper hospitals
Training rural young women as paramedical staff so doctors can concentrate on surgery
Teaching the public to carry out simple operations
questions.explain: Task-shifting means giving non-surgical tasks to trained paramedical staff, so a surgeon's scarce time is never idle.
why_wrong: The unit does not describe rotating surgeons.
The unit does not describe sending patients elsewhere.
The unit does not describe laypeople operating.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: Which Aravind lesson says free patients receive the same surgery and the same surgeons as paying ones, and only the comfort tier differs?
options: The best analogy often comes from a completely unrelated industry
Affordability can be designed
Vertical integration lowers cost
Dignity is a design requirement
questions.explain: The three lessons are the unrelated-industry analogy, affordability as an outcome of process, and dignity as a design requirement. The same-surgery point supports the third.
why_wrong: That lesson refers to the McDonald's analogy.
That lesson refers to cost coming from process as well as subsidy.
Vertical integration (Aurolab) is part of the approach, not one of the three lessons.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: Which team description is genuine Design Thinking?
options: We sat in the mess for two hours counting how long people stood in line before we proposed anything
We decided to build an attendance app, then surveyed students to find out which features they wanted in it
We picked the solution with the best technical architecture and started coding in week two
We copied a competitor's app and shipped it unchanged
questions.explain: Observing users first, before proposing anything, is the Design Thinking move. In the other options a solution is chosen before the users' problem is understood.
why_wrong: The solution (an app) was chosen first, with users asked only about features.
Technical architecture, not users, drove the choice.
Copying a product does not involve understanding users.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: In Spot the Mistake 1.1, what is the giveaway in: 'We decided to build an attendance app, then surveyed students to find out which features they wanted in it'?
options: Surveys cannot be used in Design Thinking
The solution was chosen before the users' problem was understood
The team asked too few students
Attendance is not a real problem
questions.explain: The giveaway is that the app was decided first and users were consulted only about features. That is ordinary engineering wearing a Design Thinking label.
why_wrong: Surveys can be part of research; the order of events is the problem.
The sample size is not the issue raised.
The task does not say attendance is not a real problem.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: A hostel team interviewed six residents and found the real complaint was not the food but not knowing what would be served. Why is this a good example of Design Thinking?
options: The team picked the cheapest solution first
The team avoided talking to users
