The team reframed the problem from user evidence instead of assuming it
The team replaced the food menu without testing
questions.explain: Interviewing users revealed the actual need, and the problem statement followed from evidence. That is the human-centred, user-first approach.
why_wrong: Nothing in the example concerns choosing the cheapest solution.
The team did talk to users.
No replacement of the menu took place in the example.

questions.q: A student works on a circuit problem for two hours with no progress, walks for twenty minutes, then sees the fix. What best explains this?
options: Diffuse mode reorganised the material she had already struggled with, on balance
Diffuse mode solved a problem she had never worked on before, given the scenario
Her VARK style shifted toward kinesthetic during the long walk, in this scenario
Focused mode works best only once the brain has fully rested, on the facts given
questions.explain: The unit says the diffuse mode does not work on an empty mind: it reorganises material you have already struggled with. Struggle first, then step away.
why_wrong: The diffuse mode needs earlier focused effort; it cannot solve a problem never worked on.
VARK is unrelated to the focused and diffuse rule, and its style claims lack evidence.
The unit says to alternate the modes; it does not say focused mode needs full rest.

questions.q: Which detail of the Mendeleev story matters for the unit's rule about diffuse thinking?
options: He relaxed with no earlier effort and the whole table appeared, for this team
He tested the table with real users before publishing it, taken at face value
He asked a group of colleagues to brainstorm possible layouts, as framed here
He had spent days on the problem in focused mode before the idea came, in all
questions.explain: The story is said to show dreaming, but only after days of focused work on the problem. Diffuse mode reorganises material already struggled with.
why_wrong: That reverses the story: days of focused work came first.
Testing with users is not part of the Mendeleev example.
The example is about individual focused work followed by a dream, not group brainstorming.

questions.q: Which study plan fits the unit's evidence note best?
options: Reading notes only, since her VARK result says Reading/Writing, in all
Watching videos only, since matching style lifts the results, in short
Retrieval practice, spaced sessions and mixed topics, in this scenario
Making diagrams only, since visual learners need them, on that reading
questions.explain: The unit says matching teaching to a preferred style has repeatedly failed in controlled studies. Retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving are the three strategies that do replicate.
why_wrong: Style matching is the claim that failed to hold up.
Style matching is the claim that failed to hold up.
Style matching is the claim that failed to hold up.

questions.q: A team lists seven uses for a plastic bucket, then stalls. Which move does the unit recommend next?
options: Ask more people to name uses until ideas run out, in this scenario
List the bucket's properties, then find a use for each one, in all
Pick the best of the seven and prototype it today, on that reading
Search for the bucket's official intended purposes first, in short
questions.explain: Most students stall at six or seven uses. Listing properties such as hollow, watertight, rigid, light and handled, then finding a use for each, gave twenty-eight uses in the unit's example.
why_wrong: More guessing at uses keeps the team inside the same fixed view of the object.
Prototyping now skips the exploration that breaks fixedness.
Intended purposes are exactly what functional fixedness locks people into.

questions.q: An expert says 'the method we always use has worked every time' and ignores a new proposal. Which block is this?
options: The expertise trap, since past solutions crowd out new ones, on balance
Conformity, since the expert wants to fit in with the others, in effect
Fear of failure, since the expert fears being criticised, at this stage
Premature judgment, since the idea was rejected before any test, in all
questions.explain: The expertise trap is over-reliance on past solutions: the more you know, the more you reach for what worked before.
why_wrong: Conformity is following convention in order to fit in with a group.
Fear of failure is hesitation to propose ideas because of fear of criticism.
The expert's reason is the old method's record, which is the expertise trap rather than a hasty rejection.

questions.q: A student patents a new water filter that nobody ever manufactures or uses. Which label fits the unit's definitions best?
options: Innovation, since a patent already proves it delivers value, in effect
Creativity only, since an invention must be sold to count, in practice
Disruptive innovation, since it is new and has no rivals, as described
Invention, since it is new but has not yet delivered any value, in all
questions.explain: Invention is creating something entirely new. It becomes innovation only when it is successfully implemented to create value, which has not happened here.
why_wrong: A patent is not delivered value, so it is not innovation.
Invention does not require sales; the filter exists as something new.
Disruption means transforming a market, and nothing has reached any market.

questions.q: A new charger cable keeps the old connector shape and adds faster charging. How does the unit classify this?
options: Disruptive innovation: it transforms markets with a cheaper option, based on the details
Pure creativity: an original idea that was never actually built, on the details provided
Incremental invention: a small but meaningful improvement to an existing product, in all
Functional fixedness: seeing the cable only as a charging tool, with the facts as stated
questions.explain: Incremental invention is a small but meaningful improvement to an existing product, such as USB to USB Type-C.
why_wrong: Disruptive innovation creates new markets with simpler or cheaper solutions.
The cable was built, so this is more than an unbuilt idea.
Functional fixedness is a thinking block, not a type of invention.

questions.q: Cutting urban air pollution across a state has many linked causes and no single right answer. Which kind of problem is this?
options: A well-defined problem with clear goals and one correct answer, on balance
A wicked problem, judged as better or worse, not right or wrong, in effect
An ill-defined problem that one smart design could settle for good, in all
A divergent problem that only brainstorming can ever settle, for this team
questions.explain: Wicked problems are complex and interconnected, with solutions that are better or worse rather than right or wrong. Climate, poverty and healthcare are the unit's examples.
why_wrong: Well-defined problems have clear goals, constraints and one correct answer.
Ill-defined problems have unclear goals but are not interconnected in the same way, and a single design does not settle a wicked one.
'Divergent problem' is not one of the unit's three kinds of problem.

questions.topic: History and Definition of Design Thinking
questions.q: Team A analyses a vague brief for two weeks before sketching. Team B sketches rough solutions on day one and tests them. Whose mode matches designers in Lawson's experiment?
options: Team B, since designers are solution-focused and learn through iteration, at this stage
Team A, since designers analyse the problem thoroughly before proposing answers, in all
Neither, since designers mostly copy existing solutions they know, based on the details
Both, since the mode depends only on how vague the brief is, as the scenario is set out
questions.explain: Lawson found scientists were problem-focused and designers solution-focused, creating and testing many solutions rapidly.
why_wrong: Thorough analysis first is the scientists' pattern.
The unit does not describe designers as copying existing solutions.
The experiment contrasts two ways of working, not one that depends on the brief.

questions.q: Which statement about the d.school process is correct?
options: Each stage must be fully finished before the next one can begin, in effect
Prototyping is optional when the first ideas already look strong, in short
Define comes last because it sums up every other stage, on the facts given
Testing can send a team back to empathising, so loops are expected, in all
questions.explain: The dashed arrow in the d.school diagram shows testing feeding back into empathy. The process is iterative, not linear.
why_wrong: That describes the linear waterfall approach.
Prototype is one of the five stages, and testing needs something to test.
Define is the second stage, between Empathize and Ideate.

questions.q: A product is wanted by users and buildable, but costs more than customers will pay. Which IDEO lens fails?
options: Desirability, since the people involved do not actually want it, in all
Feasibility, since the team cannot actually build it properly, in short
Viability, since the idea is not economically sustainable, as described
None, since two lenses met are enough for innovation, in this situation
questions.explain: Viability asks whether an idea is economically sustainable. Wanted and buildable but unaffordable fails the third lens, and all three must overlap for genuine innovation.
why_wrong: The scenario says users want it, so desirability is met.
The scenario says it is buildable, so feasibility is met.
The unit says meeting only one or two conditions produces a concept that fails in practice.

questions.q: A startup builds an affordable, buildable app that works well, but nobody wants it. Which lens is missing?
options: Feasibility, since the app cannot be built with today's technology, in all
Desirability, since people do not actually want what it does, in this case
Viability, since the app cannot earn enough money, on the details provided
Iteration, since IDEO's three lenses include a repeat stage, for this team
questions.explain: Desirability asks whether people want it. The scenario meets feasibility (buildable) and viability (affordable), so desirability is what fails.
why_wrong: The app is already built, so feasibility is met.
The app is affordable, so viability is not the failing lens.
Iteration is not one of the three IDEO lenses.

questions.q: What is the main risk when users only see a product at launch?
options: Late feedback makes every needed change costly to carry out, in all
Early feedback slows delivery of the first build, in this situation
Too many iterations produce a product nobody wants, on that reading
Prototypes get tested before any user need is known, as framed here
questions.explain: In waterfall each phase is finished before the next, so user feedback arrives at the end, when changes are costly. Human-centred design brings feedback in throughout.
why_wrong: That is a complaint about continuous feedback, the opposite of waterfall's problem.
Many iterations belong to human-centred design, not waterfall.
Testing prototypes before knowing needs is not what the unit describes.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: What did Airbnb's direct observation reveal that the booking data could not?
options: Listing prices in New York were too high for most guests, under the conditions given
Hosts were slow to reply, so most guests gave up waiting, in the situation described
The website loaded too slowly on phones, so guests left, as far as the scenario goes
Amateur listing photos were putting guests off, and data had not shown why, in short
questions.explain: The data showed what was happening but not why. Visiting hosts revealed poor amateur photographs, and professional photos then raised bookings.
why_wrong: Prices are not the finding of the case.
Host replies are not part of the case.
Page speed is not part of the case.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: Which outcome best supports the unit's lesson from Google Glass?
options: A lower price alone would have made it succeed anyway, as framed here
Enterprise users rejected it for the same reasons as shoppers, in all
Strong technology still failed because users did not want it, overall
Social concerns vanished once the camera was removed, on that reading
questions.explain: Technical innovation without user desirability fails: Glass sat outside the overlap of the three IDEO lenses. Price was one of several problems, not the only one.
why_wrong: The unit lists social concerns, awkward design and no clear use case alongside price.
Enterprise Edition succeeded with factory technicians.
The unit does not say removing the camera would end the concerns.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: Why did the same Glass technology get a different verdict from factory technicians?
options: Their version used cheaper hardware inside the frame, on that reading
They needed both hands free and did not mind how it looked, in effect
They were offered a much lower price than shoppers, in this situation
They had no use for a display, so only voice mattered to them, in all
questions.explain: Google relaunched Glass Enterprise Edition for warehouse and factory technicians. Same technology, different user, different verdict: a product is good or bad for someone.
why_wrong: The unit does not say the hardware changed.
The unit gives the reason as hands-free need, not price.
The unit says nothing about voice-only use.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: Which Aravind feature keeps a surgeon's scarce time from ever sitting idle?
options: Assembly-line surgery, with two tables per surgeon and task-shifting, in all
Cross-subsidy pricing, where payers choose a comfort tier, in this situation
Vertical integration, through the local lens maker Aurolab, in this scenario
Outreach camps that screen patients inside villages, on the details provided
questions.explain: Two operating tables per surgeon and task-shifting to paramedical staff keep the surgeon's time from being idle.
why_wrong: Cross-subsidy pricing is how paying patients help fund free care.
Aurolab is local lens manufacture that cuts cost.
Outreach camps remove the travel barrier through screening in villages.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: Which description is ordinary engineering wearing a Design Thinking label?
options: We changed the problem statement after three prototypes were rejected, at this stage
We counted queue times in the mess before we proposed anything, based on the details
We interviewed six residents and found the real complaint was not food, in this case
We picked the best technical architecture and began coding in week two, as described
questions.explain: A solution chosen for its architecture, with coding in week two, skips understanding users. The other descriptions start from observation, interviews or user rejection.
why_wrong: Changing the problem after user rejection is genuine Design Thinking.
Observing and counting before proposing is genuine Design Thinking.
Interviewing residents and reframing the complaint is genuine Design Thinking.

questions.topic: Case Studies: Airbnb, Google Glass, Aravind
questions.q: Which Aravind lesson says free and paying patients get the same surgery and the same surgeons?
options: The best analogy often comes from a completely unrelated industry, in this case
Affordability can be designed, as an outcome of process, from the details given
Dignity is a design requirement, so only the comfort tier differs, as described
Vertical integration lowers cost, so savings reach patients, on the facts given
questions.explain: The three lessons are the unrelated-industry analogy, affordability as an outcome of process, and dignity as a design requirement. The same-surgery point supports dignity.
why_wrong: That lesson is about the McDonald's analogy.
That lesson is about cost being designed through process.
Vertical integration is a feature of the approach, not one of the three lessons.
